# CATKit2-HCI: a collaborative framework for advancing high-contrast coronagraph testbeds

## Abstract

High-contrast exoplanet imaging requires dedicated laboratory testbeds for the development and validation of coronagraph architectures, wavefront sensing and control methods, calibration strategies, and system-level observing concepts. These testbeds often share similar software needs, yet many tools are developed independently at each institution. The CATKit2-High-Contrast-Imaging collaboration, or CATKit2-HCI, addresses this gap by providing a shared software framework for reusable HCI infrastructure. Built on top of CATKit2, an open-source hardware control and synchronization framework originally developed for the High-contrast Imager for Complex Aperture Telescopes (HiCAT) testbed at the Space Telescope Science Institute, CATKit2-HCI provides the collaborative layer for HCI-specific algorithms, calibration tools, diagnostics, visualization, and performance metrics. The collaboration currently includes multiple coronagraph testbeds in the United States and Europe. Its goals are to reduce duplicated software development, improve code quality through shared review, enable more direct comparison of results across facilities, and facilitate the movement of students, postdoctoral researchers, and collaborators between laboratories. We describe the motivation, architecture, collaboration model, shared technical capabilities, and early cross-testbed examples of CATKit2-HCI as a framework for accelerating coronagraph technology development.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

### 1.1 Scientific context and problem statement

Direct imaging and spectroscopy of exoplanets at high contrast requires the coordinated development of advanced coronagraphs, wavefront sensing and control algorithms, deformable mirror (DM) technologies, precision calibration procedures, and stable observing strategies. Laboratory testbeds play a central role in this development path by providing controlled environments in which coronagraph architectures can be assembled, calibrated, operated, and validated before similar concepts are considered for astronomical facilities or future space missions.

This laboratory infrastructure is particularly important for future exoplanet imaging missions such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO)[4, 12], for which starlight suppression must be demonstrated under increasingly realistic conditions. Similar challenges also arise for ground-based coronagraphs on current and future large telescopes, including the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).

Although individual facilities differ in aperture geometry, coronagraph architecture, DM configuration, environmental stability, wavelength range, and science goals, much of the software architecture is not fundamentally testbed-specific. High-contrast imaging (HCI) testbed teams routinely acquire and process calibration data, define dark zones, estimate focal-plane electric fields, control DMs, monitor hardware states, compute contrast metrics, and generate diagnostic plots. As the number and sophistication of coronagraph testbeds increase, shared software infrastructure becomes an enabling technology for laboratory astrophysics: common tools, interfaces, and diagnostics can accelerate progress, while their absence forces each laboratory to rebuild similar capabilities independently.

### 1.2 CATKit2 foundation

The CATKit2 package[11] provides the public hardware and service-control foundation on which CATKit2-HCI is built. It was originally developed in the context of the High-contrast Imager for Complex Aperture Telescopes (HiCAT[13]) at the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI). Its purpose is to provide a testbed-agnostic infrastructure for laboratory hardware control, including device communication, synchronization, shared memory, configuration management, and experiment orchestration.

The core design of CATKit2 is intentionally general. It provides the lower-level infrastructure needed to operate devices such as cameras, DMs, motion stages, light sources, and other laboratory hardware through a service-based architecture. This separation between hardware services and experiment logic allows testbed-specific packages to interact with devices through common service abstractions rather than ad hoc hardware scripts.

### 1.3 The missing layer

The missing layer is the software space between hardware control and private, testbed-specific science experiments. This layer includes standard HCI algorithms, calibration workflows, optical modeling utilities, diagnostics, visualization tools, performance metrics, and data products that are commonly useful across multiple coronagraphic testbeds. These tools are not raw hardware drivers, but they are also not necessarily unpublished research experiments; they form the reusable laboratory infrastructure that supports daily HCI testbed operations.

Before CATKit2-HCI, this layer was typically developed locally within each testbed repository, which made mature tools difficult to share, review, and compare. CATKit2-HCI was created to provide a common collaborative layer above CATKit2 and below the private repositories of individual testbeds.

## 2 CATKIT2-HCI COLLABORATION ARCHITECTURE AND MODEL

### 2.1 Overall concept

CATKit2-HCI is a privately shared software framework for reusable HCI infrastructure. The central idea is to separate generic laboratory capabilities from local experiments, bench-specific tuning, and unpublished science demonstrations. Each testbed retains its own repository, operating procedures, and freedom to develop new research ideas, while mature tools useful beyond a single bench can be generalized, reviewed, and proposed for migration into CATKit2-HCI.

The goal is not to force every laboratory to operate identically. Coronagraph testbeds are diverse by design, and that diversity is scientifically valuable. CATKit2-HCI instead targets the parts of the software stack where needs naturally overlap, including standard algorithms, calibration and analysis utilities, file-output conventions, plotting routines, monitoring tools, and reusable abstractions for wavefront control experiments.

### 2.2 Three-layer architecture

The CATKit2-HCI collaboration is organized around a three-layer architecture, illustrated in Fig. 1. The bottom layer is CATKit2, the public hardware and service-control infrastructure for device communication, synchronization, shared memory, configuration management, and experiment orchestration. The middle layer is CATKit2-HCI, the shared private collaboration repository containing reusable HCI infrastructure such as wavefront sensing and control algorithms, calibration and data tools, optical modeling utilities, diagnostics, plotting, visualization, and monitoring capabilities. The top layer consists of the private repositories of individual testbeds, which contain local experiments, bench-specific hardware adjustments, procedures, calibration products, unpublished science demonstrations, and configuration files.

This architecture defines a practical software boundary. CATKit2-HCI captures functionality common across HCI testbeds but too specialized to belong in the hardware-control layer. Private repositories import and extend CATKit2-HCI when appropriate while preserving the autonomy needed for each laboratory to pursue its own research program.

### 2.3 Collaboration model

The CATKit2-HCI collaboration is designed for active participation rather than passive access. The collaboration agreement asks each testbed team to contribute reusable tools, participate in technical discussions and reviews, and migrate mature, generic functionality from local repositories into the shared CATKit2-HCI layer when appropriate. It also establishes a reciprocal “rebasing” norm: when a capability has been generalized and merged into CATKit2-HCI, participating testbeds are expected to refactor equivalent local code to use the shared implementation. This principle is not intended primarily as an enforcement mechanism, but as a shared commitment to keep CATKit2-HCI technically coherent as a living common codebase rather than a set of parallel local forks.

### 2.4 Participating testbeds

The collaboration currently includes six participating coronagraph testbeds listed in Tab. 1: HiCAT[13] and CAPSULE at STScI in Baltimore; THD2[1] at LIRA / Observatoire de Paris in Meudon; SEAL[7] at the University of California, Santa Cruz; HCST[2] at Caltech in Pasadena; and ExoSPEC[8] at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt.

These testbeds span different institutions, optical architectures, and research goals. ## 3 SHARED TECHNICAL CAPABILITIES AND EARLY EXAMPLES

The framework is under active development, with mature routines being generalized from existing testbed repositories and new tools being developed directly in the shared layer. A major focus is a common software architecture for wavefront sensing and control. Many high-contrast testbeds rely on related concepts, including focal-plane wavefront estimation, probe-based electric-field sensing, and DM control. CATKit2-HCI provides a place to implement standard or classical algorithms in a reusable form, including electric field conjugation[6] (EFC), pairwise probing[5], differential Optical Transfer Function phase retrieval [3, 9], dark-zone definitions, and performance observers.

The control framework separates estimators, controllers, observers, and testbed-specific interfaces. Estimators convert image data and calibration information into quantities such as focal-plane electric-field or phase estimates. Controllers convert those estimates into commands for DMs or other actuators. Observers generate diagnostics, performance metrics, plots, and standardized outputs during or after an experiment. This abstraction makes it easier to replace one component without rewriting a full experiment, and helps different testbeds compare algorithmic choices because the same estimator or observer can be exercised in different optical environments.

CATKit2-HCI also addresses recurring needs in DM operations, data calibration, modeling, and visualization. DM utilities include actuator maps, command formatting, multi-DM abstractions, command-history storage, and readable output products. Data and calibration tools include dark calibration, auto-exposure, spot finding, image registration, contrast metrics, and image-based sampling estimates. Optical-modeling utilities include HCIPy[10]-based models, propagation helpers, standardized plotting routines, and tools for comparing modeled and measured behavior. The graphical user interface (GUI) and dashboard infrastructure supports real-time inspection of services, images, scalar time series, logs, experiments, and configurable dashboard panels, while allowing each laboratory to retain testbed-specific panels and configurations.

Two early examples illustrate the intended use of this shared layer. The first is the use of common plotting and analysis routines for EFC[6] experiments on independent testbeds, shown in Fig. 2. HiCAT and THD2 have different optical architectures and local configurations, but they share many of the same needs when evaluating wavefront control experiments: tracking contrast evolution, visualizing dark-zone performance, monitoring convergence behavior, recording DM commands, and producing diagnostic plots.

Laboratory testbeds require constant monitoring of hardware services, images, scalar values, logs, and experiment state. Historically, these tools are often built locally and can become tightly coupled to a single bench. CATKit2-HCI provides a path toward reusable monitoring components that can be configured for different testbeds. The GUI framework also reinforces a shared operational vocabulary: when teams use similar concepts for services, properties, image streams, scalar histories, and experiment execution, discussions become more efficient. Together, these capabilities reduce duplicated code, improve review, support common diagnostics, facilitate algorithm transfer, and help new contributors move more easily between laboratories. In this sense, CATKit2-HCI is both a software project and a community infrastructure project.

## 4 CONCLUSIONS

CATKit2-HCI fills the software layer between public CATKit2 hardware infrastructure and private testbed-specific experiment repositories. By collecting mature, reusable HCI tools in a shared collaboration repository, it reduces duplicated effort while preserving the flexibility needed for independent laboratory research. Its three-layer architecture and rebasing principle are intended to keep the shared codebase technically coherent without forcing all testbeds to operate identically.

Early examples from HiCAT and THD2 show how common EFC diagnostics and GUI/dashboard concepts can support cross-testbed comparison, training, and collaboration. As the framework matures, CATKit2-HCI aims to establish sustainable, community-vetted software patterns for HCI testbeds and to accelerate coronagraph technology development for future exoplanet imaging facilities, including HWO and advanced ground-based systems.

# Laboratory demonstration of low order wavefront control using light reflected off the vortex coronagraph

## Abstract

The Astro2020 Decadal Survey identified exoplanet imaging as a high priority for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), which will require imaging and characterizing exo-Earths at contrasts of $1\times 10^{-10}$ . The vector vortex coronagraph (VVC) is a leading candidate architecture for this task due to its small inner working angle and high throughput. Using light reflected from the VVC for wavefront sensing and control provides a potential path to improving robustness to residual wavefront errors and minimizing contrast degradation. The High Contrast and Spectroscopy Testbed (HCST) at Caltech’s Exoplanet Technology Laboratory (ETLab) is an in-air coronagraphic testbed that has demonstrated $1\times 10^{-8}$ broadband contrast between 3.5–10 $\lambda/D$ using a deformable mirror (DM) and a charge 8 VVC. As a first step toward full reflected light wavefront control, we present the first laboratory demonstration of a low order wavefront sensing and control (LOWFS) loop using light reflected from the VVC. This work is enabled by HCST’s recent software architecture upgrade to CATKit2, a Python-based and service-oriented framework that allows complex lab routines to run fast and concurrently. We use CATKit2 to implement phase retrieval, electric field conjugation (EFC), and the LOWFS control loop routines on HCST. Using a Gerchberg–Saxton phase retrieval routine, we reduce the science camera wavefront error from 71.6 to 7.9 nm RMS, a $>$ 9 $\times$ improvement. Over a 12 hour run with LOWFS tip-tilt tracking, we find that PSF drift is strongly correlated with bench temperature ( $r>0.88$ ). Closing the LOWFS tip-tilt loop suppresses low frequency ( $<$ 1 Hz) drift by more than two orders of magnitude, maintaining pointing precision at $<0.005~\lambda/D$ . When EFC and LOWFS are run concurrently, the closed LOWFS loop maintains a dark hole contrast of $\sim$ 5 $\times 10^{-8}$ over one hour, while the open loop case drifts by $\sim$ 0.2–0.4 $\lambda/D$ and degrades in contrast by more than one order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that tip-tilt aberrations can be sensed and stabilized using light reflected from a VVC, establishing a foundation for future reflected light wavefront sensing and control architectures for high contrast coronagraphy.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

The Astro2020 decadal survey has recommended that NASA begin the development of the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), a mission in the ultraviolet, infrared, and optical wavelengths that will search for Earth-like worlds and signs of life around other stars. In light of this recommendation, HWO will have the capability to image Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. As a technical requirement, HWO will need to achieve a contrast level of $1\times 10^{-10}$ at 3 $\lambda/D$ . Its scientific promise to directly detect and characterize Earth-like planets in reflected light depends critically on selecting a coronagraph architecture capable of both deep starlight suppression and long-term stability.

Among the leading candidates is the vector vortex coronagraph (VVC), a spiral phase mask that redistributes starlight outside the pupil while allowing nearby planetary light to pass through [10, 4]. The vortex architecture is particularly attractive because it enables small inner working angles (IWA), permitting observations closer to the star than many alternative designs [9], as well as a high off-axis throughput. However, coronagraphs are highly sensitive to wavefront error, especially tip-tilt errors that allow residual starlight to leak through and overwhelm the planet signal. To reach HWO’s required capability of imaging planets $10^{10}\times$ fainter than their stars, the telescope must continuously measure and correct for wavefront aberrations[11].

Although in theory a wavefront control architecture can help stabilize the performance of VVCs, this approach needs to be experimentally validated. In this work, we use the High Contrast and Spectroscopy Testbed (HCST) at Caltech’s Exoplanet Technology Laboratory (ETLab) to demonstrate for the first time the implementation of a tip-tilt (pointing) control loop using the light reflected off the VVC for wavefront sensing and control.

## 2 Motivation

The contrast performance of coronagraphs is highly sensitive to wavefront errors, in particular tip-tilt (pointing) upstream of the focal plane mask (FPM) in the optical path [8, 7]. There are various causes for such errors, including thermal drift, vibrations, mechanical instabilities, and, in in-air testbeds, temperature and humidity variations. These errors lead to a decreased contrast performance and stability, emerging as speckles in the final coronagraphic image. For that reason, there have been many strategies to mitigate these speckles and improve coronagraphic performance such that fainter and closer-in planets can be detected. To mitigate these effects and improve sensitivity to faint, close-in exoplanets, a variety of low-order wavefront sensing (LOWFS) strategies have been developed. These approaches differ primarily in where the sensing is performed within the optical path.

Wavefront sensing implemented upstream of the coronagraph is more susceptible to non-common path aberrations between the sensing and science channels [8]. Alternatively, sensing can be performed using light rejected or modified by the coronagraph itself, such as through reflection of the FPM [7] or by utilizing diffracted starlight at the Lyot stop [17]. These latter approaches reduce non-common path errors by probing the wavefront closer to the coronagraph, but rely on signals that have been transformed by the FPM and therefore require calibration to interpret.

Among these approaches, LOWFS architectures based on reflection at the FPM have demonstrated strong performance due to their relatively simple implementation and reduced non-common path errors [7]. This strategy has therefore been adopted for the Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) aboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [15]. However, such architectures have primarily been developed for Lyot coronagraphs and have not yet been extensively demonstrated with VVCs. Despite their theoretically perfect on-axis starlight rejection, VVCs are still sensitive to wavefront aberrations, particularly at low topological charge where the inner working angle is smallest [8]. This makes them especially promising for detecting close-in exoplanets, such as exo-Earths, while simultaneously motivating the need for robust LOWFS architectures tailored to their optical behavior.

Caltech’s HCST is ideally equipped to experimentally validate a reflection LOWFS+VVC architecture, as a LOWFS setup at the reflection off the VVC was introduced on the testbed in 2024 [3] after its optical redesign in 2023 [1].

## 3 Experimental Setup

HCST is an in-air testbed at Caltech’s ETLab. Its optical re-design is presented in [1]. Here we present HCST’s components relevant to this work and our implementation of a control loop and an electric field conjugation (EFC) algorithm with the new software architecture, CATKit2.

### 3.1 HCST’s Optical Design

The schematic of HCST is presented in Figure 1. The source assembly is a white light laser from NKT Photonics connected to a tunable filter. Other important components of HCST include a Boston Micromachines 34x34 deformable mirror (DM), a tip-tilt mirror (TTM) connected to a two axis platform by PI, a charge 8 liquid crystal polymer VVC, a Lyot stop that transmits 84% of the entrance beam, and a Hamamatsu Orca-Quest 2 qCMOS science camera (SCICAM). The LOWFS arm consists of two Thorlabs lenses with an intermediate focal plane and a Teledyne FLIR camera positioned in the final focal plane. The operating wavelength of HCST is 780 nm.

*Figure 1: HCST’s optical layout at Caltech’s ETLab. Pink rectangles represent off axis parabolic (OAP) mirrors. The 34x34 DM is 8 cm away from where the first pupil is defined. The pupil is defined by an aperture with a physical size of 10 mm. The TTM is coupled to the LOWFS readings for controlling the beam that reaches the FPM, currently a charge 8 VVC. The beam reaches the Lyot stop, which transmits 84% of the entrance beam, a Field Stop to isolate the region relevant to dark hole digging, and a low noise qCMOS ORCA Quest 2 science camera (SCICAM) manufactured by Hamamatsu.*

The LOWFS layout[3] is designed to have a magnification factor that guarantees the point spread function (PSF) is sampled above the Nyquist sampling and an intermediate focal plane such that a Zernike phase mask can be placed there in the future, with room to slide the FLIR camera to a pupil plane for full Zernike wavefront sensing. This layout will be tested and presented in future work. As of now, HCST can perform only tip-tilt sensing and control of the light reflected off the VVC. These lower order aberrations are usually the largest contributors to the degrading of coronagraphic performance.

### 3.2 CATKit2 Implementation

The previously used software architecture on HCST was the FAst Linearized COronagraph optizimer (FALCO) [16], which is MATLAB based. The main motivation for replacing the software architecture was the lack of support for running parallel control loops and its overall speed. The new software architecture, which is written in Python, is CATKit2[12]. CATKit2 uses a service oriented architecture, where each service is designed to operate a specific piece of hardware on the testbed (e.g. the TTM, SCICAM). Since Summer 2025, every piece of hardware has been integrated into CATKit2, including not only the detectors and mirrors, but also linear stages (Zaber and Thorlabs) used to align the optical components. The services operate as wrappers for each component’s SDK and make a user friendly frontend for operating the testbed. This facilitates the development of routine operations such as phase retrieval, the LOWFS PID control loop, and dark hole digging with EFC, outlined in detail in the following sections.

#### 3.2.1 Phase Retrieval

Coronagraphy relies on minimizing wavefront aberrations to produce a clean PSF for effective starlight suppression. To minimize residual aberrations from optical misalignments and imperfections on HCST, we run a phase retrieval routine between the DM and SCICAM to generate a DM “flat map” that is always applied prior to routine operations. We implement this in CATKit2 using a Gerchberg–Saxton (GS) algorithm [5].

GS is an iterative method for reconstructing wavefront phase from intensity measurements at the focal and pupil planes. HCST has a filter wheel in front of the SCICAM that allows for pupil imaging. GS carries a sign ambiguity, since $-\phi$ and $+\phi$ produce identical intensities. We break the ambiguity by repeating the retrieval at four defocus positions by moving the SCICAM on a linear stage and taking the median of the recovered phase. Starting from the measured pupil amplitude $A_{p}$ and a zero initial phase, each iteration propagates the field (with the current phase guess plus the known defocus $a_{4}Z_{4}$ ) to the focal plane,

$$ E_{f}=\mathcal{F}\left[A_{p}\,e^{i(\phi^{(k)}+a_{4}Z_{4})}\right], $$

replaces the modeled focal plane amplitude with the measured PSF amplitude while keeping the modeled phase,

$$ E_{f}^{\prime}=\sqrt{I_{\mathrm{meas}}}\,e^{i\,\phi_{f}},\quad\phi_{f}=\arg(E_{f}), $$

and propagates back to the pupil, removing the defocus term,

$$ \displaystyle E_{p} \displaystyle=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[E_{f}^{\prime}\right]\,e^{-ia_{4}Z_{4}}, \displaystyle\phi^{(k+1)} \displaystyle=\arg(E_{p}). $$

The pupil amplitude is then reimposed and the process repeats. We run 300 GS iterations per defocus image and apply the resulting correction over 6 rounds at a gain of $0.7$ to avoid overcorrection.

GS recovers a phase map on a pupil grid, but the DM correction must be applied on the $34\times 34$ actuator grid, whose orientation does not match the SCICAM. To map between the two, we poke a $3\times 3$ block of actuators at five positions across the DM and locate the pokes with GS (Figure 2). The five DM–pupil coordinate pairs are fit with a 2D affine transform,

$$ \displaystyle x_{\mathrm{pup}} \displaystyle=0.108\,c+3.629\,r-1.2, \displaystyle y_{\mathrm{pup}} \displaystyle=-3.558\,c+0.057\,r+125.2, $$

where $(r,c)$ are actuator row and column indices and $(x_{\mathrm{pup}},y_{\mathrm{pup}})$ are pixel coordinates on the $128\times 128$ GS phase grid. The mapping gives a scale of 3.59 pupil pixels per actuator and a rotation of $-88^{\circ}$ between the DM and pupil coordinate systems, set by the orientation of the DM relative to the SCICAM.

*Figure 2: Mapping the pupil (top) to DM (bottom) coordinates.*

With this calibration, the GS phase is sampled at each actuator’s mapped position by linear interpolation,

$$ \phi_{\mathrm{DM}}(r,c)=\phi_{\mathrm{GS}}\!\left(y_{\mathrm{pup}}(r,c),\;x_{\mathrm{pup}}(r,c)\right), $$

and converted to a surface height. We deconvolve the DM actuator’s influence function from the target surface to recover the actuator commands that reproduce the desired shape.

#### 3.2.2 PID Tip-Tilt Control Loop

The LOWFS re-images the PSF incident on the VVC onto a FLIR camera (see Figure 3), allowing us to monitor residual tip-tilt jitter and drift of the PSF relative to the vortex center (see Figure 1, blue optical path). The LOWFS sampling is approximately 5.2 pixels per $\lambda/D$ . The TTM, located upstream of the VVC, is used to correct this motion by steering the PSF back to the VVC center.

*Figure 3: Left: The PSF image for the LOWFS system, which is obtained via the reflection of the PSF off the VVC (blue light path in Figure 1). It is sampled at 5.2 pixels/ $\lambda$ /D. The asymmetries arise due to aberrations caused by our two lens system. Right: PSF image from our SCICAM. It is oversampled at about 10.3 pixels/ $\lambda$ /D.*

The PSF position is measured on each frame using both Gaussian and center of mass centroiding. A reference centroid is first established when the PSF is aligned to the VVC center. We assess the behavior of the centroid in both open loop (tracking) and closed loop (controlling). During the closed loop operation, the measured centroid is compared against this reference position to form an error signal,

$$ \mathbf{e}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t)-x_{0}\\
y(t)-y_{0}\end{bmatrix}, $$

where $(x_{0},y_{0})$ is the reference centroid corresponding to the VVC center. This error signal is then passed to a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller. The PID control law is

$$ u(t)=K_{p}e(t)+K_{i}\int_{0}^{t}e(\tau)\,d\tau+K_{d}\frac{de(t)}{dt}, $$

where $u(t)$ is the controller output, $e(t)$ is the centroid error, and $K_{p}$ , $K_{i}$ , and $K_{d}$ are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains. In our implementation, the controller is applied independently to the measured $x$ and $y$ centroid errors. The proportional gain is set to 0.15 and the integral gain to 0.002. The derivative gain was set to zero, so the final controller is a PI controller. To convert centroid corrections into TTM commands, we calibrate the response of the LOWFS centroid position to small TTM motions. Because there can be cross-coupling between the X and Y axis on the TTM, we model the response with a $2\times 2$ interaction matrix,

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\
\Delta y\end{bmatrix}=J\begin{bmatrix}\Delta B\\
\Delta A\end{bmatrix},\qquad J=\begin{bmatrix}\partial x/\partial B&\partial x/\partial A\\
\partial y/\partial B&\partial y/\partial A\end{bmatrix}. $$

$\Delta A$ and $\Delta B$ are small TTM actuator offsets, and $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the resulting centroid shifts measured on the FLIR. We determine $J$ by applying small calibration pokes of 0.05 mrad to each TTM axis and measuring the corresponding centroid displacement. The inverse matrix $J^{-1}$ is then used during closed loop operation to convert the desired LOWFS centroid correction into TTM actuator commands.

#### 3.2.3 Dark Hole Digging with EFC

Alignment alone is not sufficient to reach levels of $10^{-8}$ on the testbed. In order to dig a dark hole where higher contrast can be achieved, we implement an EFC [6] routine using CATKit2 on HCST. On HCST, the dark hole is a D-shaped region spanning 4.5–10 $\lambda/D$ (the previous FALCO baseline was 3.5–10 $\lambda/D$ ). EFC is a model-based approach to sense and minimize the electric field in a region on the SCICAM. At each iteration, the focal plane electric field is estimated using pairwise probing. A set of known DM probe shapes is applied with positive and negative signs, and the resulting intensity differences are used to infer the complex field in the dark hole. Given this estimate, the EFC update is computed from the linearized model

$$ \Delta E\approx G\Delta u, $$

where $G$ is the Jacobian mapping DM actuator commands to focal-plane electric-field changes and $\Delta u$ is the incremental DM command. We solve for $\Delta u$ using a regularized least squares controller and apply the correction with a scalar gain to maintain stable closed-loop behavior on the testbed.

The measured contrast is computed from dark-subtracted coronagraphic images normalized by the direct PSF peak and corrected for exposure time,

$$ C=\frac{(I_{\mathrm{coron}}-I_{\mathrm{dark}})t_{\mathrm{direct}}}{I_{\mathrm{direct,peak}}t_{\mathrm{coron}}}. $$

The contrast reported for each iteration is the mean of $C$ over the D-shaped dark hole region.

## 4 Experimental Results

Here we present our results on the implementation of the phase retrieval, LOWFS tip-tilt control and EFC on HCST using the CATKit2 software architecture.

### 4.1 Phase Retrieval

We quantify the residual aberration using the root-mean-square wavefront error (WFE RMS), defined as the standard deviation of the optical path difference over the illuminated pupil. Lower WFE RMS corresponds to a wavefront closer to the ideal reference surface. Our phase retrieval algorithm using 6 rounds of GS with a defocus offset to break sign ambiguity takes our PSF from WFE RMS from 71.6 to 7.9 nm (see Figure 4), which corresponds to a $>$ 9 $\times$ reduction in the starting WFE for the SCICAM. The full process from testbed initialization to final PSF takes 18 minutes. The DM surface displacement was estimated using a local voltage-to-height calibration of 1.13 $\mu\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{V}$ , a value obtained from previous calibration on HCST. Because the MEMS actuator response is nonlinear over its full command range, this factor does not represent a global stroke calibration.

### 4.2 Tip-Tilt Tracking and Control off of the VVC: Performance Results

In this section, we present our tip-tilt tracking and control results using the LOWFS system at the reflection of the VVC.

#### 4.2.1 Environmental Data

We monitor the temperature and humidity on HCST using small sensors inside the bench to determine whether variations in these environmental parameters are correlated with drift of the PSF. To test this, we tracked the PSF centroid for 12 hours in open loop while simultaneously recording the temperature and humidity inside the testbed. The environmental data is reported at 0.1 Hz, and the tip-tilt data is reported at 100 Hz. For that reason, we average the data from both components every 1 minute in order to assess potential correlations. Figure 5 shows the measured tip-tilt drift and temperature variation, along with their correlations.

To quantify the correlation between the environmental variations and the measured tip-tilt drift, we compute the Pearson correlation coefficient, defined as

$$ r_{xy}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_{i}-\bar{x})(y_{i}-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}}, $$

where $x_{i}$ is the environmental variation, either $\Delta T$ or $\Delta H$ , and $y_{i}$ is the measured one-minute mean tip-tilt centroid position. The quantities $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ are the corresponding sample means. A value of $r=1$ indicates a perfect positive linear correlation.

We find significant correlations ( $>$ 0.888) between the drift and temperature during the 12 hour run. The temperature varied $>$ 0.5∘ overnight, with a sudden temperature increase around 8 hours into tracking leading to a reversal in the tip-tilt drift direction. For humidity, there is also a level of correlation ( $>0.69$ for every variable), but not as high as for temperature, where levels of correlation consistently reached $\gtrsim 0.9$ . The humidity varied by 0.4 $\%$ during our 12 hour run. From these results, we conclude that drift on HCST is mostly due to thermal and humidity changes on the testbed.

The correlation coefficient, computed here as the Pearson r, shows a correlation factor of near 1, confirming the drift is likely caused by temperature changes on the testbed.*

#### 4.2.2 Tip-Tilt Control

After finding significant drift of our PSF due to environmental parameters, we implement the PID control loop presented in Section 3.2.2 on the LOWFS, while simultaneously tracking the centroid on the SCICAM. We run the loop for 12 hours and compare to our open loop results from Section 4.2.1. Our results are shown in Figure 6. We find a significant improvement of more than two orders of magnitude in the LOWFS drift at frequencies below $1~\mathrm{Hz}$ along both axes, with a consistent pointing precision of $<0.005~\lambda/D$ .

The closed loop correction does not appear to improve the drift measured on the SCICAM, whose PSD remains essentially unchanged between the open and closed loop cases, and drift levels remain comparable to the open loop. Since there are many optics between the LOWFS and the SCICAM, there is a possibility of non-common path aberrations between the two PSFs. However, the purpose of the LOWFS control loop is to eliminate drift upstream of the VVC, since pointing errors upstream of the coronagraph are among the dominant contributors to degraded contrast and contrast stability. For this reason, the effectiveness of the control loop can ultimately only be assessed when it is run concurrently with EFC.

#### 4.2.3 Dark Hole Digging + LOWFS on reflection of the VVC

Here we present the results of our first implementation of EFC on HCST with CATKit2, and its parallel operation with the LOWFS. Our goal is to assess how much the tip-tilt drift found in the previous section can potentially affect our contrast stability.

Our EFC implementation in CATKit2 reaches contrast levels of $\sim$ 5e-8 in a dark hole region between 4.5 – 10 $\lambda/D$ at 780 $\pm$ 10 nm wavelengths. We use three pairs of sinc function probes for redudancy in order to estimate the local electric field in the SCICAM. HCST’s previous baseline with FALCO for a dark hole region of 3.5 – 10 $\lambda/D$ was 1e-8 [2], suggesting our CATKit2 HCST implementation has a mismatch between the optical model of the testbed and the true bench response, which is being investigated. However, we noticed a significant increase in the EFC iteration speed since our switch to CATKit2: previously, 50 EFC iterations with FALCO would take $\sim$ 30 minutes, while with CATKit2 it takes $<$ 15 minutes, a factor of 2 increase. Due to its service-based architecture, CATKit2 should be able to dig a dark hole within a few seconds, rather than minutes [12], suggesting there are remaining overheads in our current implementation. Potential overheads remaining involve a complex wrapper around the EFC loop, in particular for sending probes. In the future, our goal is to turn the entire EFC loop (and LOWFS loop) into a standalone CATKit2 service, essentially eliminating any additional overheads.

CATKit2 allows for multiple complex loops to occur simultaneously on the testbed. We implement a combination of EFC + tip-tilt control in order to monitor/control the PSF pointing on the FPM with the LOWFS and TTM, while simultaneously using the SCICAM and the DM to dig a dark hole with EFC. In order to assess stability of our tip-tilt control while EFC is operational, we run 30 iterations of EFC and continuously monitor the contrast in the dark hole region for 1 hour. We run this test for two cases: LOWFS tracking (open loop) and control (closed loop). Similarly to the previous section, we find a large drift ( $>$ 0.1 $\lambda/D$ ) in the open loop case, while the closed loop remains $\sim 0.005\lambda/D$ at all times.

However, the presence of the drift on the testbed is not ideal for long-term operations, even with LOWFS control, and it was not always present in the lab [2]. We believe the tip-tilt mirror itself is drifting due to temperature changes, since it is the only component that changed from 2024 to now. ## 5 Discussion & Future Work

We have presented initial experimental results of a LOWFS tip-tilt control system operating at the reflection of a charge 8 VVC on HCST, implemented within the new CATKit2 software architecture. Our phase retrieval routine reduces the SCICAM wavefront error from 71.6 to 7.9 nm RMS, a $>$ 9 $\times$ improvement, and produces the flat map that now seeds all routine operations on the testbed. Closing the tip-tilt loop on light reflected from the VVC suppresses low frequency drift by more than two orders of magnitude, taking residual pointing from $\sigma\approx 0.20/0.14~\lambda/D$ in open loop to $\lesssim 0.005~\lambda/D$ in closed loop. Most importantly, when EFC and the LOWFS loop are run concurrently, the closed loop holds pointing near $0.005~\lambda/D$ and maintains a dark hole contrast of $\sim$ 5 $\times 10^{-8}$ , whereas in open loop a drift of $\sim$ 0.2–0.4 $\lambda/D$ degrades the contrast by more than an order of magnitude over the same interval. Together these results demonstrate for the first time that pointing can be sensed and stabilized at the reflection of a VVC, and that doing so plays a meaningful role in coronagraphic contrast stability.

Several tests remain to be conducted. First, we will continue to trace the sources of drift on the bench beyond temperature, in particular isolating whether the tip-tilt mirror itself is drifting due to thermal effects or a software or hardware issue, since it is the dominant change to the testbed since 2024 when drift levels were minimal [2]. Second, we will quantify and reduce the mismatch between our optical model and the true bench response that currently limits our CATKit2 EFC contrast relative to the prior FALCO baseline, focusing on DM registration and orientation and Lyot stop alignment. The goal is to establish a baseline previously found on HCST prior to the tip-tilt mirror installation and transition to CATKit2, which was a mean dark hole contrast of 1e-8 between 3.5–10 $\lambda/D$ . Third, we plan to reimplement the EFC loop (and the LOWFS loop) as standalone CATKit2 services to eliminate any remaining software overhead and enable dark hole digging at much higher cadence alongside LOWFS control, approaching the few-second dark-hole-digging times that CATKit2 should allow [13]. Once these are resolved, we will test apodizers[14] for HWO and update the DM electronics, both of which we expect to further validate the LOWFS+VVC architecture as a candidate for HWO.

## Abstract

Different theories of dark matter predict different populations and morphologies of galactic subhaloes below about $10^{8}M_{\odot}$ . The planned angular resolution and optical stability of the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) should enable it to detect subtle subhalo perturbations in strongly lensed galaxy images. We simulate 2000-second exposures with its High Resolution Imager (HRI) under the fiducial Exploratory Analytic Case 1 (EAC1) design, assuming known source structure and omitting lens-galaxy light. Pre-selecting the top 50 of 965 lenses (5.2%) using only arc signal-to-noise and relative gradient power lowers the median mass threshold for 10% aperture coverage roughly tenfold relative to the full ensemble. The top 12 (1.2%) reach a median of $6.6\times 10^{7}M_{\odot}$ for the same coverage. At their most sensitive positions, the top 50 and top 12 reach median thresholds of $3\times 10^{7}M_{\odot}$ and $1.5\times 10^{7}M_{\odot}$ , respectively. Non-linear fits support the Fisher forecasts at the tested masses and positions. For these 12 lenses, increasing the physical wavefront error from 35 to 65 nm RMS raises the median thresholds by only 0.1 dex when the point spread function (PSF) is modelled correctly. Deliberately mismodelling the 35-nm reference PSF removes detectable positions, although false detections remain rare. Under our illustrative retention criteria, loss of sensitive area sets a median tolerated wavefront mismatch of 5 nm RMS (range 2–10 nm). Selective HWO follow-up of lenses discovered by Euclid or Roman could therefore transform our understanding of the nature of dark matter, provided that the PSF is characterized accurately enough to preserve this sensitivity.

## 1 Introduction

Various theories of dark matter predict vastly different morphologies and populations of dark matter subhaloes. In a nearly homogeneous universe with small overdensities, an overdense region can attract surrounding matter. Cold dark matter (CDM) predicts dark matter particles with small primordial random velocities, where negligible free streaming on galactic scales is expected. This leads to CDM collapsing into these overdense regions, where some merge into the larger galaxy-sized haloes and others remain as smaller subhaloes (Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin, 2017). Warm dark matter (WDM) predicts dark matter particles with larger primordial random velocities compared to CDM, leading to larger free streaming (Bode et al., 2001). This leads to the suppression of small-scale primordial overdensities as particles stream out of the smallest overdense regions, reducing the density contrast before gravity can amplify these regions into haloes. Small-scale fluctuations are smoothed, while larger-scale overdensities cannot be sufficiently suppressed in time, and instead form larger galaxy-sized haloes. As a result, WDM predicts a much smaller number of low-mass subhaloes compared to CDM (Lovell et al., 2014). Therefore, measuring subhalo populations, especially at low masses, can be a powerful probe into the theoretical nature of dark matter (Vegetti et al., 2014).

Gravitational lensing has proven to be a powerful tool for detecting these dark matter subhaloes (Vegetti et al., 2010). The ’strong’ gravitational lensing regime is characterized by the extreme distortions of background sources that are closely aligned with the lensing object in the line of sight. These sources can form extended arcs of light around the lensing object when the background source is extended, or multiple imaging when the background source is compact, such as a quasar. We can directly model the paths the light rays from these sources must travel around the lens galaxy using general relativity (Bartelmann, 2010). But when dark matter subhaloes are present in the lens galaxy, these subhaloes can act as additional lenses of the background source light, creating localized distortions in the spatial brightness pattern. We can numerically model these distortions and thus can detect the presence of these low-mass perturbers to attempt to distinguish between competing dark matter models (Vegetti & Koopmans, 2009).

However, detection of low-mass subhaloes in the regime where these theories meaningfully diverge is challenging. The lensing system has many parameters to consider, and all must be inferred jointly to search for the substructure (Vegetti & Koopmans, 2009). These components can explain part of the suspected subhalo perturbation signal: adjusting the macro lens model changes the lensing geometry, and adjusting the source model changes the brightness structure that is being mapped (Despali et al., 2022). In a similar vein, overly restrictive model assumptions can generate confident, but incorrect, subhalo evidence (He et al., 2023). Therefore, trustworthy analysis requires physically justified model flexibility, even if this reduces the detection significance. Fine structure that carries information about low-mass perturbers can be further degraded by finite angular resolution (Despali et al., 2022), while fine detector sampling is also needed to preserve that spatial information delivered by the optical system. Point spread function (PSF) variations can also alter the apparent substructure signal (Wedig et al., 2025). Consequently, these challenges motivate observations that combine high angular resolution and sufficient signal-to-noise with a stable, accurately characterized PSF.

The upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) may be an ideal instrument to fill many of these requirements. HWO is a NASA flagship-level mission concept designed in response to the Astro2020 decadal survey (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2023). Its primary goal is to directly image nearby Earth-like exoplanets, enabled by extremely high-contrast coronagraphy and extremely stable instrument optics (Liu et al., 2026). Although its name highlights the search for habitable worlds, HWO is also intended to support a broad astrophysics programme (Dressing et al., 2026). Candidate instruments for this broader programme include a High Resolution Imager (HRI) and an ultraviolet multi-object spectrograph (UV-MOS), enabling investigations from planetary to cosmological scales (Liu et al., 2026). With the space-based, ultra-stable optics required for the coronagraphy alongside the HRI, HWO is well suited to carry out a low-mass subhalo detection programme to distinguish between various theories of dark matter (He et al., 2026).

Even with HWO’s proposed capabilities, the sensitivity to low-mass subhaloes will vary between different lens systems. Despali et al. (2022) have shown that even with the same observational setup, maximum sensitivity can depend dramatically on the source structure and lens geometry. Wedig et al. (2025) have forecasted that the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s High Latitude Wide Area Survey (HLWAS) alone will discover approximately 160,000 lensing systems, which would motivate a future HWO strong lensing programme to perform follow-up observations over the systems with the highest expected subhalo information content (O’Riordan et al., 2023). PSF quality will be a critical factor in the success of detecting these low-mass subhaloes with statistical significance. Two distinct optical questions for forecasting such a programme arise: how does the sensitivity change when the physical PSF degrades but remains correctly modelled (PSF quality), and how does it change when the PSF is mismodelled (PSF knowledge error)?

In this work, we quantify how mass reach varies across lensing systems and how PSF quality and modelling accuracy affect subhalo detection sensitivity for HWO’s Exploratory Analytic Case 1 (EAC1) architecture (Liu et al., 2026). To simulate and forecast HWO’s subhalo detection sensitivity case, we use the HWO Strong Lensing Analysis Pipeline for Subhaloes (HWO-SLAPS) (Vassilakis et al., 2026). This pipeline, which is open-source on GitHub11 1 https://github.com/nasa-jpl/hwo-slaps, simulates the subhalo detection sensitivity case end-to-end. HWO-SLAPS builds a galaxy-galaxy lensing system, injects or omits a subhalo into the lens galaxy, then convolves that scene with selected HWO-like PSFs and adds detector and measurement noise to create a mock observation. These mock observations are then analysed through two complementary approaches: fast Fisher/Asimov likelihood-ratio forecasts (Cowan et al., 2011) and targeted non-linear model comparisons, which yield likelihood ratios (Nightingale et al., 2021a; Lange, 2023). In this study, we generate 1000 lensing systems spanning a range of source and lens properties and compute Fisher sensitivity maps for the 965 systems that pass our observability cuts. We test these forecasts with targeted non-linear fits to the 50 highest-ranked systems and a pseudorandom validation sample of 100 systems, including no-subhalo controls to assess false-positive detections. We also explore the effect of the PSF on these detection metrics through two separate arms: varying physical PSF quality with correct modelling and introducing controlled PSF knowledge errors. Under declared observing conditions, these foreground-free simulations provide a controlled baseline for exploring the feasibility of a potential HWO low-mass subhalo detection programme.

The paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 describes the simulation suite and lens population. Section 3 defines the detection metrics and validation protocol. Section 4 presents the mass-reach and target-selection results alongside the non-linear validation set. Section 5 examines the effects of PSF quality and knowledge errors on subhalo detection sensitivity. We discuss the implications and limitations in Section 6 and summarize our conclusions in Section 7.

### 2.2 Lens and subhalo models

Within the HWO-SLAPS pipeline, we use PyAutoLens (Nightingale et al., 2021a) to model and simulate all aspects of the lensing system, including the source, lens, and subhalo. We model the lens galaxy as having a large-scale mass distribution, denoted the macro lens, which is chiefly responsible for the strong lensing effect, while a smaller-scale mass profile, denoted the subhalo, lives within the macro lens and is optionally added to the simulation. We represent the macro lens as a singular isothermal ellipsoid (SIE) mass distribution (Kormann et al., 1994), whose dimensionless projected surface mass density is given by

$$ \displaystyle\kappa(\xi) \displaystyle=\frac{\Sigma(\xi)}{\Sigma_{\rm crit}}=\frac{\theta_{\rm E,eff}}{2\xi},\qquad\Sigma_{\rm crit}=\frac{c^{2}}{4\pi G}\frac{D_{\rm s}}{D_{\rm l}D_{\rm ls}}, \displaystyle\xi^{2} \displaystyle=q_{\rm lens}\,x^{\prime 2}+\frac{y^{\prime 2}}{q_{\rm lens}}, $$

where $\kappa$ is the convergence, $\Sigma$ is the projected surface mass density, and $\Sigma_{\rm crit}$ is the critical surface density for the lens–source system. Here $D_{\rm s}$ , $D_{\rm l}$ , and $D_{\rm ls}$ are the observer–source, observer–lens, and lens–source angular-diameter distances, respectively. The constants $c$ and $G$ are the speed of light and Newton’s gravitational constant, respectively. The angular coordinates $x^{\prime}$ and $y^{\prime}$ are centred on the lens and aligned with its projected major and minor axes, respectively, with $q_{\rm lens}$ denoting the minor-to-major axis ratio and $\xi$ the corresponding elliptical radius. We define $\theta_{\rm E,eff}=\sqrt{A_{\rm crit}/\pi}$ as the area-equivalent Einstein radius, where $A_{\rm crit}$ is the angular area enclosed by the tangential critical curve.

The adopted cosmology is the spatially flat $\Lambda$ CDM model implemented as Planck15 within PyAutoLens, with $H_{0}=67.74\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ and $\Omega_{\rm m}=0.3075$ (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016). The SIE represents the combined smooth mass of the lens galaxy, including both baryonic and dark matter, without an additional external-shear component. We keep the SIE model family fixed, while allowing its centre, mass normalization, and ellipticity to adjust in the non-linear search, as described in Section 3.

The subhalo follows a spherical Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW) profile (Navarro et al., 1997) and is placed at the same redshift as the lens galaxy. Its three-dimensional density is given by

$$ \rho(r)=\frac{\rho_{s}}{(r/r_{s})(1+r/r_{s})^{2}}, $$

where $r$ is the physical radius from the subhalo centre, $r_{s}$ is the scale radius, and $\rho_{s}$ sets the density normalization. The density approaches $\rho\propto r^{-1}$ at small radii and $\rho\propto r^{-3}$ at large radii, with a logarithmic slope of $-2$ at $r=r_{s}$ . We define the subhalo mass ( $M_{200}$ ) and concentration ( $c_{200}$ ) as

$$ \displaystyle M_{200} \displaystyle=\frac{4\pi}{3}\,200\,\rho_{\rm crit}(z_{l})\,r_{200}^{3}, \displaystyle\rho_{\rm crit}(z_{l}) \displaystyle=\frac{3H(z_{l})^{2}}{8\pi G}, \displaystyle c_{200} \displaystyle=\frac{r_{200}}{r_{s}}, $$

where $r_{200}$ is the physical radius enclosing a mean density of $200\rho_{\rm crit}(z_{l})$ , and $H(z_{l})$ is the Hubble parameter at the lens redshift. Here $\rho_{\rm crit}$ is the cosmological critical volume density, distinct from the lensing critical surface density $\Sigma_{\rm crit}$ . The concentration $c_{200}$ is the ratio of $r_{200}$ to the scale radius $r_{s}$ . At fixed $M_{200}$ and redshift, a higher concentration $c_{200}$ places more of the mass within the smaller projected radii, strengthening the lensing perturbation which can increase the detection significance (Amorisco et al., 2022).

We set $c_{200}$ using the concentration mass relation defined in equation (7) of Moliné et al. (2017), which depends on $M_{200}$ and $x_{\rm sub}$ , the three-dimensional distance from the host centre in units of the host virial radius. This relation assigns higher concentrations to subhaloes that are closer to the centre of the host halo. We set $x_{\rm sub}=1$ independent of the subhalo’s projected position, which is a conservative choice compared to higher concentrations predicted for subhaloes that are embedded deeper within the host. The relation was calibrated at $z=0$ for Milky Way-mass hosts, and we apply it without any redshift-evolution term or intrinsic scatter. The lens redshift therefore only enters through $\rho_{\rm crit}(z_{l})$ in equation (3) and through the lensing distances in $\Sigma_{\rm crit}$ in equation (1).

Throughout this study, subhalo mass refers to $M_{200}$ , the mass enclosed within $r_{200}$ . The spherical NFW profiles remain untruncated, as in Nightingale et al. (2024). The subhalo mass and projected position are varied systematically to map detection sensitivity across the lensing systems described in Section 2.4. This suite of simulations considers the effects of placing a single subhalo at the lens redshift, with no additional population of haloes along the line of sight.

### 2.3 Source models

Different source morphologies will lead to different gradient structures in the lensed image, and this can affect the detection significance of the subhalo (Despali et al., 2022). Motivated by this, we use five source templates spanning a clumpy galaxy, a barred spiral, an irregular galaxy, a compact galaxy, and a smooth disc. These templates are based on F814W images taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) for the COSMOS survey (Koekemoer et al., 2007), obtained from the real-galaxy sample distributed for GalSim (Rowe et al., 2015). The five source templates are shown in the top row of Fig. 1.

Each image is background-subtracted, masked to isolate the galaxy, and centred on its light centroid, with negative pixel values set to zero. The angular scale is then adjusted so that a circular aperture of radius 0.11 arcsec contains half of the retained light. This provides a common reference size before the source sizes, orientations, and positions are assigned as described in Section 2.4. During ray tracing, bilinear interpolation gives the source surface brightness at each mapped source-plane position. The templates are used without deconvolving the original HST PSF and retain residual observational noise.

We anchor the source brightness to the average unlensed F814W magnitude of 24.3 reported in the Sloan Lens ACS (SLACS) survey (Newton et al., 2011). An adopted colour of $m_{\rm HRI-V}-m_{\rm F814W}=0.545$ gives a reference HRI-V magnitude of 24.845. Each template is initially normalized to the corresponding unlensed detected rate of $8.95\,\mathrm{e}^{-}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ under the observing conditions in Section 2.1. The magnitudes and sizes of individual sources are drawn as described in Section 2.4. When a source is resized, its surface-brightness normalization is adjusted to preserve the total flux at its assigned magnitude. Lensing magnification is generated by ray tracing and is not applied during source normalization. The five templates thus provide a controlled range of source structures for the mass reach analysis, without modelling the full source population or changes in morphology with wavelength or redshift.

### 2.4 Lens population and target selection

We generate an initial pool of 1000 lensing systems using the sampling prescriptions listed in Appendix A (Table 6). We balance the allocation of systems by source morphology, assigning 200 systems per template. The pool allows the exploration of a controlled range of lens geometries and source properties to compare mass reach and target selection.

The lens and source redshift distributions are centred at $z_{\rm l}=0.22$ and $z_{\rm s}=0.65$ , respectively, motivated by the typical SLACS lens and source redshifts (Newton et al., 2011). The lens velocity dispersion and lens-source distances determine the Einstein radius of the lens. Source placement is specified by their angular offset from the lens centre, which we express as a fraction of this radius. We draw this fraction from a log-uniform distribution, emphasizing close alignments within the strong lensing regime. Source magnitudes are drawn from a normal distribution centred on the SLACS-based reference magnitude of 24.845 described in Section 2.3. The full sampling distributions and their bounds are provided in Appendix A.

Next, we identify targets from the initial 1000-system pool that are likely to have the highest low-mass subhalo sensitivity, using only their images before any sensitivity is measured. This represents a follow-up style programme in which HWO observes the highest-ranked lensing systems from a population of hundreds of thousands of systems, as expected from Euclid and Roman’s lensing surveys (O’Riordan et al., 2023; Wedig et al., 2025). Bright arcs provide more signal and brightness gradients can make small deflections more visible, so we construct a selection score based on these properties. Each system is rendered without a subhalo, using the observing conditions described in Section 2.1. From this expected image, we calculate the integrated arc signal-to-noise ratio $\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}$ , noise-weighted gradient power $G_{\rm abs}$ , and dimensionless relative gradient power $G_{\rm rel}$ within a circular aperture of radius $2\theta_{\rm E,eff}$ centred on the lens:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{s_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}, \displaystyle G_{\rm abs} \displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{|\nabla s_{i}|^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}, \displaystyle G_{\rm rel} \displaystyle=\frac{\theta_{\rm res}^{2}G_{\rm abs}}{\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}^{2}}, $$

where $s_{i}$ is the expected source electron count in pixel $i$ and $\sigma_{i}^{2}$ is its variance under the noise model in Section 2.1. The gradient is taken with respect to angular position, and $\theta_{\rm res}=\lambda/D$ is expressed in arcseconds, with $\lambda=500$ nm and $D$ the circumscribed pupil diameter. Making an image brighter increases its gradient power even when spatial structure is unchanged. By dividing $G_{\rm abs}$ by $\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}^{2}$ , we reduce this increase in gradient power caused by brightness alone, although some brightness dependence remains due to relative pixel weights changing with source brightness.

Following the sample-selection cuts used by O’Riordan et al. (2023), we retain systems with $\theta_{\rm E,eff}>0.5$ arcsec and $\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}>20$ , leaving 965 systems. These are ranked by

$$ \mathcal{R}=\mathcal{Z}(\log\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc})+\mathcal{Z}(\log G_{\rm rel}). $$

Here, $\mathcal{Z}$ denotes the z-score, calculated by subtracting the mean and dividing by the population standard deviation across the 965 surviving systems. The ranking score therefore gives equal weight to the z-scores of log signal-to-noise ratio and log relative gradient power. The score was fixed before measuring injected-subhalo sensitivity, and in Section 4, we assess how well this ranking predicts subhalo sensitivity.

We assess the gain from target selection by comparing the mass reach of the 12, 25, 50, and 100 highest-ranked systems with that of the full ensemble of 965 survivors. Fisher sensitivity maps are calculated for all 965 systems (Section 3.2). The top 50 form the selected sample for the non-linear comparisons (Section 3.3), and the top 12 form the sample for the PSF tests in Section 5. To test the Fisher forecasts beyond the highest-ranked systems, we select a pseudorandom validation sample of 100 systems from the full surviving ensemble, without using the selection score or measured subhalo sensitivity (Appendix A). Seven members also belong to the top 50, making up a total of 143 systems with non-linear fits. The ranking is fixed using only the expected subhalo-free images, intentionally set before evaluating subhalo sensitivity.

### 2.5 Point spread function model

We generate the PSFs with the High Contrast Imaging in Python (HCIPy) package (Por et al., 2018), using the EAC1 pupil described in Section 2.1. The aberrated PSF combines both global Zernike modes over the pupil and hexagonal Zernike (hexike) modes within individual mirror segments. Hexikes form an orthonormal polynomial basis on a hexagonal pupil (Mahajan & Dai, 2006), and we contributed their segmented implementation into HCIPy for this project. The model uses global Noll indices 4–55 and the first ten segment modes, including piston, tip, and tilt. HCIPy then propagates the pupil wavefront to the focal plane at 500 nm. The intensity is integrated over the image pixels and each detector-sampled kernel is normalized to unit total flux.

We derive the relative mode weights from publicly available optical path difference (OPD) maps produced by JWST wavefront sensing (Lajoie et al., 2023), retrieved from the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST) through the STPSF package33 3 https://stpsf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jwst_measured_opds.html. We decompose each map into global Zernike modes over the full pupil, then fit hexike modes within each segment to the residual. Individual OPD maps determine the static weights, while differences between consecutive maps, excluding pairs that span a commanded mirror correction, determine the drift weights. The fitted JWST coefficients thus determine the weights of the individual modes and the balance between global and segment aberrations. Each mode coefficient is drawn from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution whose width is proportional to its derived weight. The combined wavefront is then rescaled to a desired RMS optical path difference over the illuminated EAC1 pupil.

The PSF-quality experiment varies the RMS amplitude of the reference wavefront, using the resulting PSF to both generate and model the images. For the PSF-knowledge experiment, the simulated images retain the reference PSF, corresponding to 35 nm RMS wavefront error, while an additional wavefront error is introduced into the fitted PSF. This error is generated using the drift weights and scaled to a prescribed RMS before being added to the reference wavefront; the amplitudes are chosen for this study rather than predicted for HWO. Section 5 presents the resulting changes in subhalo sensitivity.

## 3 Detection metrics

In this section, we define the metrics used to quantify subhalo detection sensitivity. To limit the computational cost, we use the Fisher approximation for sensitivity maps and reserve non-linear fits for targeted validation. We first describe the Fisher detection statistic (Section 3.1), then explain how sensitivity maps give the mass thresholds used to compare lens systems (Section 3.2). Finally, we describe the non-linear fits used to test these forecasts (Section 3.3).

### 3.1 Fisher detection statistic

Small changes to the macro lens and source parameters can reproduce part of the image perturbation caused by a subhalo. Allowing these parameters to adjust is therefore necessary to avoid overstating the subhalo detection significance. Initially motivated by computational constraints, we develop a Fisher approximation to evaluate the residual subhalo signal across a wide set of subhalo masses and positions without a full non-linear search at each point.

The agreement between the observed and modelled pixels is quantified by the Gaussian log likelihood

$$ \log\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\eta})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\frac{[d_{i}-m_{i}(\boldsymbol{\eta})]^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}+\mathrm{constant}, $$

where $d_{i}$ and $m_{i}$ are the observed and modelled electron counts in pixel $i$ , $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ is the vector of lens, source, and background parameters, and $\sigma_{i}^{2}$ is the pixel variance. The variances follow the noise model in Section 2.1 with derived values from the parameters in Table 1. These variances are fixed when comparing between smooth and subhalo models.

To determine whether the measurement favours a subhalo, we compare the best-fitting smooth model with a model that includes a subhalo. The improvement in fit is quantified by the likelihood-ratio statistic

$$ q=2\left(\log\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{subhalo}}-\log\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{smooth}}\right)=\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{smooth},\min}-\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{subhalo},\min}, $$

where the hats denote maximized likelihoods, and $\chi^{2}$ is the noise-weighted sum of squared image residuals. For the Fisher forecasts, the data $d_{i}$ are the expected electron counts in the simulated image containing a subhalo. These are referred to as Asimov data (Cowan et al., 2011), with observational noise accounted for through the pixel variances $\sigma_{i}^{2}$ in the likelihood.

The Fisher calculation includes ten nuisance parameters: the lens centre, Einstein radius, and two ellipticity components; the source centre, flux normalization, and size; and a constant background offset. The source template’s internal structure and rotation remain fixed, as does the PSF, and no priors are imposed on the nuisance shifts.

For each trial subhalo mass $M=M_{200}$ and lens-plane position $\boldsymbol{x}$ , we calculate the PSF-convolved image containing the subhalo. Its difference from the corresponding smooth image is $\Delta m_{i}(M,\boldsymbol{x})$ . The response of the smooth model to small parameter shifts is approximated by a first-order expansion about the input parameters $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}$ :

$$ m_{\mathrm{smooth},i}(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}+\delta\boldsymbol{\eta})\simeq m_{\mathrm{smooth},i}(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0})+\sum_{j}J_{ij}\,\delta\eta_{j}, $$

where $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}$ contains the input smooth-model parameters, and $\delta\eta_{j}$ is a shift in nuisance parameter $j$ . The image Jacobian $J$ has elements $J_{ij}=\partial m_{\mathrm{smooth},i}/\partial\eta_{j}$ , evaluated at $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}$ , describing how the modelled count in pixel $i$ changes with parameter $j$ . The two terms of equation (7) then simplify for different reasons. The input subhalo model reproduces the Asimov data exactly, so $\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{subhalo},\min}=0$ . In the smooth term, equation (8) makes the residual linear in the nuisance parameter shifts. Minimizing that residual over the shifts gives the Fisher statistic $q_{\mathrm{F}}$

$$ q_{\mathrm{F}}(M,\boldsymbol{x})=\min_{\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}\sum_{i}\frac{\left[\Delta m_{i}(M,\boldsymbol{x})-\sum_{j}J_{ij}\,\delta\eta_{j}\right]^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}. $$

We evaluate the statistic over all pixels of the simulated image, allowing the nuisance parameters to adjust jointly in the minimization.

To evaluate equation (9), we find the combination of nuisance parameter shifts that best reproduces the subhalo perturbation. This separates the perturbation into the part that the smooth model can absorb and the residual that remains. Because the residual is linear in the nuisance shifts, this minimization has a closed-form solution, avoiding a non-linear search over the parameters. The solution is determined by the nuisance Fisher matrix $F=J^{\mathsf{T}}C^{-1}J$ , where $C=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{i}^{2})$ is the image-noise covariance matrix. The Fisher matrix describes how strongly the image constrains different combinations of nuisance parameters. The best-fitting shifts are $\widehat{\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}=F^{+}J^{\mathsf{T}}C^{-1}\Delta\boldsymbol{m}$ , where $F^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $F$ and handles nuisance directions that leave the image unchanged. Substituting them into equation (9) gives

$$ q_{\mathrm{F}}=\Delta\boldsymbol{m}^{\mathsf{T}}C^{-1}\Delta\boldsymbol{m}-\widehat{\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{\mathsf{T}}F\,\widehat{\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}. $$

The first term measures the noise-weighted strength of the perturbation with the smooth model held fixed. The second subtracts the contribution reproduced by the best-fitting nuisance shifts, leaving the signal that remains unexplained within the linear approximation.

We adopt $q_{\mathrm{F}}\geq 10$ , a log-likelihood gain of 5, following the detection threshold of the HWO strong-lensing science case (He et al., 2026). This statistic defines the sensitivity maps of Section 3.2 and is tested against non-linear fits in Section 3.3.

For the PSF-modelling-error tests in Section 5.2, the images are generated with the true PSF but modelled with an incorrect PSF. This mismatch can leave $\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{subhalo},\min}$ nonzero, so the assumption used to reduce the likelihood ratio to equation (9) no longer holds in general. We therefore retain both terms of equation (7) and evaluate them using the linear approximation in equation (8). Let $r_{i}=d_{i}-m_{\mathrm{smooth},i}$ be the residual between the true expected image and the smooth image calculated with the fitted PSF. We compute the nuisance responses $J_{ij}$ and the trial subhalo perturbation $\Delta m_{i}$ with the same fitted PSF. We fit a scale factor $a$ to adjust the strength of the trial subhalo perturbation when matching it to the residual image, giving

$$ \displaystyle q={} \displaystyle\min_{\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}\sum_{i}\frac{\left[r_{i}-\sum_{j}J_{ij}\,\delta\eta_{j}\right]^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}} \displaystyle-\min_{a,\,\delta\boldsymbol{\eta}}\sum_{i}\frac{\left[r_{i}-a\Delta m_{i}-\sum_{j}J_{ij}\,\delta\eta_{j}\right]^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}. $$

The first term fits the smooth model alone; the second also includes the scaled subhalo perturbation, with the nuisance parameters allowed to readjust. Either a positive or negative amplitude can improve the fit, but a negative amplitude reverses the predicted subhalo perturbation. We therefore require the best-fitting amplitude $\hat{a}>0$ as well as $q\geq 10$ . Using the true expected image with or without a subhalo as $d_{i}$ gives the injection or no-subhalo map, respectively. In images without a subhalo, positions satisfying these conditions count as false detections. With a correct PSF and an injected subhalo, $r_{i}=\Delta m_{i}$ , the second term vanishes at $a=1$ , and $q$ reduces to $q_{\mathrm{F}}$ in equation (9).

### 3.2 Sensitivity maps and mass thresholds

Although subhalo mass reach is the standard strong lensing literature statistic, the mass of a subhalo does not determine its detectability alone. The lensing geometry and source morphology of a given system determine where a subhalo produces a measurable perturbation. We evaluate $q_{\mathrm{F}}(M,\boldsymbol{x})$ on a grid of ‘trial’ subhalo positions spaced by $\Delta x=0.05$ arcsec, within a $2\theta_{\rm E,eff}$ radius centred on the lens. The population has a range of area-equivalent Einstein radii $\theta_{\rm E,eff}$ of $0.5$ to $3.05$ arcsec, so we scale the aperture with $\theta_{\rm E,eff}$ so that the area fractions can be compared between lenses. This choice of aperture, including the factor of $2$ , follows O’Riordan et al. (2023) who report sensitive-area fractions within $2\theta_{\rm E}$ for Euclid. Evaluating $q_{\mathrm{F}}$ across these positions gives both the lowest mass a system can reach and how much of the aperture is sensitive at each mass.

At each mass, the sensitive area $A(M)$ is the total area of the trial cells satisfying $q_{\mathrm{F}}\geq 10$ , and $f(M)$ is the fraction of cells that pass this threshold within the total aperture,

$$ A(M)=N_{\rm det}(M)\,(\Delta x)^{2},\qquad f(M)=\frac{N_{\rm det}(M)}{N_{\mathcal{A}}}. $$

Here, $N_{\rm det}(M)$ is the number of trial positions inside the aperture with $q_{\mathrm{F}}(M,\boldsymbol{x})\geq 10$ , and $N_{\mathcal{A}}$ is the total number of trial positions inside it. We repeat this calculation over $10^{6}\leq M_{200}/M_{\odot}\leq 10^{9.5}$ in steps of 0.25 dex to estimate three mass thresholds for each system. $M_{\rm best}$ is the lowest mass at which $q_{\mathrm{F}}$ reaches $10$ at any evaluated position. $M_{10}$ and $M_{50}$ are the masses at which $f(M)$ reaches 0.10 and 0.50, respectively, allowing us to distinguish between absolute low-mass reach of a system and one that is sensitive over a larger area. The angular area corresponding to 10% aperture coverage is $0.1N_{\mathcal{A}}(\Delta x)^{2}\simeq 0.1\pi(2\theta_{\rm E,eff})^{2}$ , while the area for 50% coverage is five times larger. Table 7 gives the median, mean, and range of the 10% areas for the full ensemble and the selected samples. Figure 3 shows these three areas for a sample system. Additional 0.1-dex steps are added around the $M_{\rm best}$ crossing to achieve finer mass thresholding. Since the $q_{\mathrm{F}}\geq 10$ thresholds can fall between the sampled masses, we interpolate linearly in log mass between the two sampled masses on either side of the crossing. If the detection threshold is not reached by $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ , we stop the search and record it as a lower bound, still retaining its place in the overall range for the computation of medians.

### 3.3 Non-linear model comparisons

We test the Fisher forecasts with non-linear fits that allow finite changes to the lens and source parameters. Each image is fitted with PyAutoLens (Nightingale et al., 2021a) using a smooth lensing system model and the same model with a subhalo. Both the SIE model family and the source template’s internal structure and rotation are fixed, allowing a controlled comparison with the Fisher calculation. The centre, Einstein radius, and ellipticity of the lens are free, as are the centre, flux, and size of the source, within uniform priors centred on the input values (Table 2). The widths are informed by the default prior-passing settings of the Source, Light and Mass (SLaM) pipelines in PyAutoLens, which are used by He et al. (2023) and Nightingale et al. (2024). The subhalo has the NFW profile and concentration defined in Section 2.2, with a log-uniform mass prior between $10^{6}$ and $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ . Its centre varies about the test position by $\pm 0.15$ arcsec in each coordinate.
