Since the highest-likelihood sample need not locate the maximum precisely, we refine each fit with bounded L-BFGS-B optimization (Byrd et al., 1995) in SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020) from multiple starting points. Twice the signed difference between the subhalo and smooth-model log-likelihood maxima gives $q_{\mathrm{fit}}$ (equation (7)), and we require $q_{\mathrm{fit}}\geq 10$ for detection. Before classifying a comparison, we check that both maxima are repeatable and agree with independent likelihood calculations. If either fit fails these checks, we repeat both searches once with more thorough sampling and apply the same refinement and checks. Comparisons that still fail are reported as unresolved, without a detection classification. The sampler settings and numerical checks are given in Appendix B.

We hold the supplied PSF fixed in each non-linear fit. The non-linear fits use a $51\times 51$ -pixel PSF kernel and exclude a border of half the kernel width, where the convolution is incomplete. With the $999\times 999$ -pixel kernel of the production Fisher maps, this border would cover most of each image. The fits also subtract the known background, whereas the Fisher maps allow a background offset to vary. We compare $q_{\mathrm{fit}}$ with the production Fisher prediction at the same test mass and position. For the top 12, we also calculate the linearized statistic using the same kernel, fitted pixels, noise weights, and background treatment as the non-linear fits. This separates the effect of non-linear adjustment from the differences in image treatment.

We apply these fits to the 143 systems defined in Section 2.4. Asimov injections test the Fisher approximation using expected images, while noisy injections test recovery in individual noise realizations. We use no-subhalo controls to measure false detections. Each system has one noisy injection and one corresponding control. For the top 50, nine additional control realizations give ten controls per system and 500 in total.

For each system, the test mass is the upper sampled mass bracketing the correct-PSF $M_{\rm best}$ crossing in the production Fisher maps. Systems without a crossing are tested at the upper sampled limit of $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ . At this mass, we recompute the Fisher map using the kernel of the non-linear fits and define the test position as the aperture position, clear of the excluded border, where the statistic is largest. The Asimov and noisy injections share this mass and position, and the control uses the same local search window without an injected subhalo. For the top 12, we also use the Asimov injection at the lower bracketing mass, with its position selected independently by the same rule at that mass. Together, the two masses give the 24 Asimov comparisons in Section 4.3. The PSF-error tests in Section 5.3 reuse the top-12 injection and control images while changing the supplied PSF. These non-linear comparisons test selected masses and positions, while the $M_{10}$ and $M_{50}$ thresholds are derived from the full Fisher sensitivity maps.

## 4 Subhalo detection sensitivity

In this section, we present the subhalo detection sensitivity and mass reach of the lens population when the 35 nm RMS reference PSF is modelled correctly. We first describe the distribution of mass thresholds across the 965 surviving systems and the five source templates (Section 4.1), then examine how pre-detection selection by $\mathcal{R}$ changes the mass reach (Section 4.2). Finally, we validate the Fisher forecasts against targeted non-linear fits (Section 4.3).

### 4.1 Subhalo mass sensitivity

Figure 4 shows the cumulative distributions of $M_{\rm best}$ , $M_{10}$ , and $M_{50}$ for the 965 surviving systems and each source template. The lowest detectable threshold in any system is $M_{\rm best}=10^{7.02}M_{\odot}$ , reached at a single position in a system using the clumpy source template. The median $M_{\rm best}$ of the entire ensemble is $10^{8.62}M_{\odot}$ (Table 3). Compared to the median $M_{\rm best}$ , requiring the subhalo to be discoverable across a breadth of area raises the mass meaningfully. Within the sampled mass range, 142 systems cannot detect a subhalo at any evaluated position. For the area thresholds, 269 and 377 systems cannot detect a subhalo over 10% and 50% of the aperture, respectively. These systems remain in the distributions and median calculations.

Three cumulative distributions compare mass thresholds across source templates. Requiring greater aperture coverage shifts the distributions towards higher masses. Barred-spiral systems generally reach lower masses, while smooth-disc systems reach higher masses. Curves ending below one hundred per cent indicate unreached thresholds.

Each template represents only one galaxy of its morphology class, not a source morphology population, so these comparisons do not isolate the cause.

The template alone does not determine the mass reach of an individual system. Although the barred-spiral and smooth-disc medians differ by a full dex, 17 of the 193 smooth-disc systems reach a lower $M_{\rm best}$ than the barred-spiral median. ### 4.2 The effect of target selection

The ranking statistic $\mathcal{R}$ was designed in the spirit of a follow-up programme that selects targets before observation and subsequent subhalo detection (Section 2.4). Figure 5 shows that the mass thresholds generally increase with pre-detection rank, indicating that $\mathcal{R}$ , combining $\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm arc}$ and $G_{\rm rel}$ , identifies configurations with lower thresholds. Across all 965 systems, the Spearman correlations between numerical rank and $M_{\rm best}$ , $M_{10}$ , and $M_{50}$ are 0.93, 0.86, and 0.82, respectively (systems with thresholds unreached at $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ are placed after all measured thresholds, tied with one another). Within each source template, the $M_{\rm best}$ correlation is 0.90–0.92, so the ranking also orders configurations that share a template. The lowest value of each threshold occurs within the top ten, though not at pre-detection rank 1, and all of the 200 highest-ranked systems reach all three thresholds.

For the top 50 systems, the median thresholds are $M_{\rm best}=10^{7.51}M_{\odot}$ , $M_{10}=10^{8.12}M_{\odot}$ , and $M_{50}=10^{8.54}M_{\odot}$ (Table 3), which are approximately 1.1, 1.0, and 0.8 dex below the ensemble medians, respectively. For $M_{10}$ , this top-50 pre-detection selection results in a factor of ten better mass reach. The top 12, which form the sample for the PSF tests in Section 5, reach further, with medians of $M_{\rm best}=10^{7.19}M_{\odot}$ , $M_{10}=10^{7.82}M_{\odot}$ , and $M_{50}=10^{8.30}M_{\odot}$ . The gain declines slowly with sample size, as seen in Table 3. The top 50 contains no smooth-disc systems, but 19 of its members use the irregular and compact templates, whose ensemble medians track the full population (Section 4.1). The ranking therefore selects favourable configurations within these templates as well as the templates with the lowest thresholds. We do not propose $\mathcal{R}$ as the statistic a future HWO programme would use; it stands in for selecting the most favourable systems from a larger sample. Because it is computed from the noise-free expected images, the selection gain realized by a future programme depends on how well these systems can be identified from noisy survey images. The top 50 forms the selected sample for the non-linear tests in Section 4.3.

### 4.3 Comparison with non-linear fits

Figure 6 shows the agreement between the Fisher and non-linear statistics for the top 50 systems and a randomly drawn validation sample of 100 systems. Seven systems drawn from the 965-system population overlap with the top 50, giving 143 distinct systems in total. All 50 Asimov injections in the selected sample satisfy $q_{\mathrm{fit}}\geq 10$ , with $R^{2}=0.988$ for a linear fit between the two statistics. The median difference $q_{\mathrm{fit}}-q_{\mathrm{F}}$ is $+0.41$ relative to the production maps. Most of this offset is accounted for by the likelihood conventions of the non-linear fits (Section 3.3). For the top 12, a linear calculation using the same kernel, border, and background treatment as the fits lies a median of 0.39 above the production prediction and differs from $q_{\mathrm{fit}}$ by less than 0.043 across the 24 upper- and lower-mass Asimov tests. The linear approximation therefore holds at these masses and positions, and the non-linear adjustment of the lens and source changes $q$ very little.

The validation sample shows where this tight agreement degrades. Of the 81 validation-only systems that the Fisher calculation predicts to be detectable, 69 are detected in the non-linear Asimov fits. All 12 misses occur at masses between $10^{9}$ and $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ , above every top-50 test mass. These discrepancies are consistent with larger adjustments of the lens and source absorbing more of the perturbation than the linear approximation in the Fisher calculation allows. Despali et al. The threshold disagreements in Fig. 6 run in one direction: no system is detected by the non-linear Asimov fit but not by Fisher. The selection ranking that improves mass reach (Section 4.2) also identifies systems for which the two statistics agree.

## 5 PSF degradation and mismodelling

Section 4 used the 35 nm RMS reference PSF and assumed that it is perfectly modelled. In this section, we relax that assumption and examine how PSF quality and modelling errors affect the 12 highest-ranked systems selected in Section 4.2. We first vary the physical PSF while modelling it correctly (Section 5.1), then keep the true PSF fixed and introduce modelling errors in the fitted PSF (Section 5.2). Finally, we test how these errors change subhalo recovery and false detections in the non-linear fits (Section 5.3).

### 5.1 The effect of PSF degradation

Figure 7 shows how the three mass thresholds change when the reference wavefront (Fig. 2) is scaled from 0 to 65 nm RMS, with the resulting PSF used both to generate and to model each image. The sampled amplitudes span an unaberrated PSF at 0 nm, an optimistic HWO case at 20 nm, the 35-nm reference, a degraded case at 50 nm, and 65 nm, comparable to the in-flight wavefront error of JWST (Lajoie et al., 2023). The 35-nm reference meets the Maréchal criterion for diffraction-limited imaging at 500 nm (Strehl ratio $\geq 0.8$ ).

The 35-nm RMS point corresponds to the top-12 row of Table 3. Relative to this reference, an unaberrated PSF lowers the median $M_{\rm best}$ , $M_{10}$ , and $M_{50}$ by only 0.05, 0.04, and 0.04 dex, respectively, while increasing the wavefront error to 65 nm raises them by 0.11, 0.11, and 0.09 dex. The Strehl ratio falls from 1 at 0 nm to 0.84 at 35 nm and 0.57 at 65 nm as aberrations move light out of the PSF core and reduce the contrast of fine image structure in the lensing system. Across this wavefront-error range, the changes in mass reach are substantially smaller than the variation among the 12 systems and the approximately 1-dex gain from target selection in Section 4.2.

### 5.2 The effect of PSF modelling errors

To test how PSF knowledge affects subhalo sensitivity, we use the 35-nm reference PSF in the simulated images and add a drift-shaped wavefront error to the fitted PSF, following Section 2.5. For each of the 12 systems, we draw eight error patterns, referred to as directions, and scale each to 1, 2, 5, 10, and 20 nm RMS. We evaluate sensitivity at the upper sampled mass bracketing each system’s correct-PSF $M_{\rm best}$ , $M_{10}$ , and $M_{50}$ thresholds. We compute the sensitivity maps with equation (11), which measures how strongly the remaining image residuals resemble a subhalo after allowing first-order adjustments to the nuisance parameters.

PSF modelling errors can suppress or strengthen the fitted subhalo signal, changing which positions on the lens are sensitive. This is shown in Fig. 8. For the highest-ranked system with an injected subhalo mass of $10^{8}M_{\odot}$ , the displayed 10-nm error leaves only 79% of the originally sensitive positions above the threshold, while increasing the total sensitive area by 11%. The corresponding no-subhalo map remains below $q=10$ throughout the aperture. The additional crossings occur only in the injected maps and indicate an increased apparent preference for a subhalo under the incorrect PSF.

To measure how much of the original sensitivity survives, we define $K$ as the fraction of correct-PSF sensitive positions that remain above threshold with the incorrect PSF. We also define $F$ as the area satisfying $\hat{a}>0$ and $q\geq 10$ in the no-subhalo map, divided by the correct-PSF sensitive area at the same mass. Both quantities are computed from the expected images. As illustrative performance criteria, we require $Q_{10}(K)\geq 0.9$ and $Q_{90}(F)\leq 0.1$ , where $Q_{p}$ is the $p$ th percentile over the eight directions. At these percentiles, we require at least 90% of the originally sensitive area to remain detectable, while limiting the area producing false detections to 10% of that same original area. We define each system’s tolerance as the largest sampled error amplitude satisfying both criteria, and apply these criteria at the $M_{10}$ and $M_{50}$ test masses.

Under these criteria, all 12 systems pass at 2 nm and most at 5 nm (Table 5). At 10 nm, only four systems pass at the $M_{10}$ test masses and two at the $M_{50}$ test masses, and none pass at 20 nm. Most systems therefore have a tolerance of 5 nm: seven of the 12 in the $M_{10}$ tests and eight in the $M_{50}$ tests pass at 5 nm and fail at 10 nm. Every system satisfies the $F$ criterion at every sampled amplitude, so loss of the original sensitive positions sets the tolerances.

### 5.3 Non-linear fits with PSF modelling errors

We test whether the response to PSF modelling errors in the Fisher maps persists in non-linear fits to noisy images of the 12 highest-ranked systems. Three of the eight error directions are tested at 2, 5, 10, and 20 nm RMS, giving 36 conditions per amplitude. Each injection and control image is held fixed relative to its correct-PSF counterpart in Section 4.3, so changes within a pair must arise from the PSF used in fitting. Only one condition detected with the correct PSF is lost for errors up to 10 nm, first falling below threshold at 5 nm. Increasing the error to 20 nm leaves 28 of the 33 initially detected conditions, with the five losses confined to two systems (Table 5). Every non-linear loss also falls below threshold in the Fisher map at the same test mass and position. At 20 nm, the Fisher calculation predicts 11 lost detections, compared with five in the non-linear fits. For the 11 systems detected with the correct PSF, the median Fisher statistic is 10.8, just above the detection threshold of 10, whereas the median statistic from the noisy non-linear fits is 14.0. The Fisher predictions therefore require a smaller decrease to fall below threshold, which may help explain the additional predicted losses.

PSF modelling errors also increase $q_{\mathrm{fit}}$ in 22–24 of the 36 injected conditions at each amplitude. At 20 nm, changes relative to the correct-PSF fits span $-8.8$ to $+24.7$ . These increases represent a greater apparent preference for the subhalo model but do not produce any newly detected injections in these tests.

None of the 12 correct-PSF controls produces a false detection, and no accepted control fit crosses the threshold for PSF errors up to 10 nm. A false detection appears in one of the 36 controls when the error reaches 20 nm. For this control and error direction, increasing the PSF error on the same noisy image raises $q_{\mathrm{fit}}$ from 4.0 to 11.2. The non-linear tests therefore support the picture from the sensitivity maps, with PSF modelling errors causing missed detections while false detections remain rare within the tested search windows.

## 6 Discussion

The HWO strong-lensing science case of He et al. (2026) identifies sensitivity to dark matter haloes near $10^{7}M_{\odot}$ as a route to testing alternatives to CDM. The study considers detection programmes of 500 to 2000 lensing systems. Wide-field surveys will discover far more lenses than such a programme can observe, with approximately 170,000 forecast for Euclid (Collett, 2015; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2026) and 160,000 for Roman’s HLWAS (Wedig et al., 2025). The reach of a programme therefore depends on how well the most sensitive systems can be pre-selected for deep follow-up. Under common observing conditions, the 50 highest-ranked systems in our ensemble have a median $M_{\rm best}$ of $10^{7.51}M_{\odot}$ , about 1.1 dex below the ensemble median, and the median for the 12 highest-ranked systems is $10^{7.19}M_{\odot}$ . For scale, our top-50 and top-12 samples represent 5.2% and 1.2% of the simulated ensemble. Selecting the same fractions of the forecast Euclid or Roman populations would give samples of approximately 8,000–9,000 and 2,000 lenses, respectively. How many of the forecasted survey lenses reach these thresholds depends on various lens property factors that our population does not reproduce, such as the redshift, brightness, Einstein radius, and source morphology distributions. The variation in sensitivity across lens configurations therefore motivates identifying those most suited to low-mass subhalo searches before allocating HWO programme time.

For a future HWO follow-up programme, the aim would therefore be to identify promising targets from the larger survey population before following up and calculating their subhalo sensitivity. Pre-selecting the top 50 by $\mathcal{R}$ lowered the median $M_{10}$ from $10^{9.11}$ to $10^{8.12}M_{\odot}$ in our analysis, so the gain extends to the area over which subhaloes are detectable as well as the aforementioned $M_{\rm best}$ thresholds. O’Riordan et al. (2023) demonstrated the value of selecting lenses by the depth or area of their sensitivity maps, while our score uses arc signal-to-noise and relative gradient power measured directly from the expected images. Applying it to survey candidates would require estimating these quantities from noisy images with lower resolution than the HWO follow-up data will provide, and the realized gain will depend on how well the informative structure can be identified in these images.

Full non-linear fits become computationally expensive when repeated across many lens systems, subhalo masses, positions, and observational configurations. Our comparisons show that the faster Fisher approximation closely reproduces the non-linear detection statistics at the masses and positions tested in the selected sample. All 50 selected systems are detected in the Asimov fits at their upper test masses and chosen positions. For the top 12, a linear calculation using the same PSF kernel, pixels, and background treatment as the non-linear fits gives Fisher statistics that differ from the non-linear values by less than 0.043. The threshold disagreements in the validation sample occur at $10^{9}$ – $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ , above every test mass in the selected sample, consistent with the larger lens and source adjustments absorbing more of the perturbation than the linear approximation in the Fisher method predicts. Fisher maps are therefore well suited for larger sweeps of observing configurations at low subhalo masses, with non-linear fits confirming these forecasts at selected positions and masses. Most injections are tested just above the Fisher detection threshold, so noise can push some just below it.

The PSF experiments in this study respond to He et al. (2026), who identified precise PSF knowledge as essential for this science case and left the required PSF stability for future work. We test this by analysing how wavefront error affects the information in the image and how accurately the PSF must be modelled to recover it. For the top 12 systems, degrading the physical wavefront error from 35 to 65 nm RMS raises the median mass thresholds by about 0.1 dex along the tested wavefront pattern when the PSF is modelled correctly. Wedig et al. (2025) also found a modest effect in deep Roman imaging, where with detector sensitivity held fixed, the mean minimum subhalo mass detectable at $3\sigma$ varies by about 5% across the focal plane and tracks the wavefront error. Their idealized $\chi^{2}$ statistic attributes every image difference to the subhalo, without refitting the lens or source. An incorrect PSF model can also introduce residuals that resemble a subhalo perturbation or cancel part of the fitted subhalo signal. This cancellation removes one of the 33 correct-PSF detections at 5 and 10 nm RMS, and five at 20 nm. Positions can also cross the detection threshold without any improvement in the observed image. Changing the fitted PSF can increase the apparent preference for a subhalo, although false detections remain rare in these tests. Only one of the 143 accepted PSF-error control comparisons crosses the detection threshold, at 20 nm RMS, where the statistic rises from 4.0 with the correct PSF to 11.2 on the same noisy image.

In the Fisher maps, loss of originally detectable positions sets the PSF-modelling tolerance. Under the illustrative criteria in Section 5.2, the median tolerance is 5 nm RMS, with a range of 2–10 nm across the 12 systems for both the $M_{10}$ and $M_{50}$ tests. The tolerances describe the mismatch between the true and assumed wavefronts in the model, with no time-scale attached. Our PSF-error patterns use relative mode weights derived from differences between consecutive JWST OPD measurements. Lajoie et al. (2023) report a median measured change of 9 nm RMS over 48 hours during Cycle 1, including sensing noise estimated at 5–7 nm RMS. Our median tolerance of 5 nm RMS is comparable to that sensing noise and smaller than the median measured two-day change.

We generate and fit each image using the same source template and family of SIE lens mass models where the lens and source parameters can adjust, but the source’s internal structure remains fixed. In observations, all structure must be inferred from the data, which can give the source model more freedom to absorb part of a subhalo perturbation. He et al. (2023) showed that this additional freedom can reduce both subhalo sensitivity and false positives. The lens mass model can also leave residuals that resemble a subhalo if it cannot reproduce the underlying mass distribution, leading to false detections or biased masses, as shown by He et al. (2023) and Nightingale et al. (2024). We also omit lens-galaxy light, as in the simulated lenses of He et al. (2023), and Despali et al. (2022) found that including correctly modelled lens light did not alter their sensitivity results. These effects can interact with PSF errors because each changes the residuals that the subhalo model fits. These forecasts are therefore optimistic with respect to source reconstruction and foreground light.

Our adopted concentrations are lower than the Moliné et al. (2017) relation predicts for subhaloes nearer the host centre (Section 2.2). More concentrated haloes, including those above the relation when scatter is included, could be detected at lower masses (Amorisco et al., 2022). The thresholds also describe sensitivity to individual subhaloes in the lens plane, and constraining dark matter would additionally require the abundance of perturbers, including haloes along the line of sight, and the selection of the observed lenses. Baryonic processes can also alter subhalo abundances and internal structure (Porras-Bedmar et al., 2026). Fits with reconstructed sources and lens light would test how much of the reach of the selected systems remains in a more complete analysis. Ranking simulated survey images would test whether the selection gain carries over to real candidates, and recovering PSFs from simulated HWO calibration observations would test whether the required modelling accuracy can be achieved. A search over the full arc with its own controls would similarly test the false-positive rate.

## 7 Conclusions

Following the HWO strong-lensing science case of He et al. (2026), we have used HWO-SLAPS to forecast subhalo sensitivity for 965 simulated lens systems under a common 2000-s HWO EAC1/HRI observation, and tested how PSF quality and modelling errors affect the 12 highest-ranked systems. Ranking the systems by arc signal-to-noise and relative gradient power before calculating subhalo sensitivity gives a top-50 median $M_{\rm best}$ of $10^{7.51}M_{\odot}$ , about 1.1 dex below the ensemble median, and $10^{7.19}M_{\odot}$ for the top 12. Selection also lowers the median $M_{10}$ from $10^{9.11}$ to $10^{8.12}M_{\odot}$ , so the approximately one-dex gain extends to the mass detectable over 10% of the aperture. Our ranking uses noise-free expected images, and realizing this gain in a follow-up programme depends on identifying the same arc signal-to-noise and relative gradient power in survey images.

Non-linear fits detect all 50 selected Asimov injections at their tested masses and positions. For the top 12, linear and non-linear calculations with the same image treatment closely agree, showing that finite lens and source adjustments change the detection statistic very little. The 12 validation systems that the Fisher maps predict as detectable but the non-linear fits miss are tested at $10^{9}$ – $10^{9.5}M_{\odot}$ , above every test mass in the selected sample. With one noise realization, 38 of the 50 selected injections are recovered, consistent with testing close to the detection threshold. These comparisons support using Fisher maps to explore many systems and observing configurations, with non-linear checks at selected masses and positions.

For the top 12 systems, increasing the physical wavefront error from 35 to 65 nm RMS raises the median mass thresholds by about 0.1 dex when the PSF is modelled correctly. Errors in the fitted PSF can instead remove detectable positions and increase the apparent preference for a subhalo, although only one of the 143 accepted PSF-error controls gives a false detection. Under our illustrative retention criteria, the median tolerated wavefront mismatch is 5 nm RMS, with a range of 2–10 nm across the systems. These forecasts assume known source structure and omit lens-galaxy light, so they are optimistic in these respects. The adopted subhalo concentrations are instead conservative, since subhaloes nearer the host centre or above the median relation would be easier to detect. These results support selective HWO follow-up of the large lens samples expected from Euclid and Roman. With accurate PSF modelling to preserve sensitivity to low-mass subhaloes, such a programme could transform our understanding of the nature of dark matter.

## Appendix B Numerical procedure of the non-linear fits

The Nautilus searches in Section 3.3 use 300 live points for the smooth model and 600 for the subhalo model, with a minimum effective-sample target of $n_{\rm eff}=2000$ and a limit of $2\times 10^{6}$ likelihood evaluations per model. For optimization, we rescale each parameter to $[0,1]$ using its prior bounds (Table 2). The sampler’s maximum-likelihood point supplies one starting point. We select eight further samples in descending likelihood order, requiring separation from every previously selected point by a Euclidean distance of at least 0.05 in these coordinates, or at least one after scaling each coordinate by its weighted posterior standard deviation.

From each starting point, bounded L-BFGS-B minimizes $\chi^{2}/2$ using gradients obtained by automatic differentiation. Each run allows 500 iterations and 50 line-search steps per iteration, with a gradient tolerance of $10^{-10}$ and zero function tolerance. We retain the highest likelihood encountered across the runs, then repeat the optimization from that point with 1000 iterations and a gradient tolerance of $10^{-12}$ . We accept a maximum only if at least two of the eight additional starts reach log likelihoods within 0.1 of it and the tighter repeat changes it by no more than 0.1. The retained point must have a finite gradient. Its noise-weighted residual sum of squares must agree with the optimizer’s $\chi^{2}$ to within $10^{-4}$ , and its directly evaluated log likelihood must agree with that implied by the optimizer to the same tolerance. We also check that the sampler’s maximum reproduces its saved log likelihood to within $10^{-4}$ .

If either model fails these checks, we repeat both searches once with a fresh sampler seed, doubling the number of live points, the effective-sample target, and the likelihood-evaluation limit. This gives 600 live points for the smooth model, 1200 for the subhalo model, $n_{\rm eff}=4000$ , and a limit of $4\times 10^{6}$ likelihood evaluations per model. The images, priors, refinement procedure, and acceptance checks remain the same. We adopt this second comparison only if both models pass and neither log-likelihood maximum falls more than 0.1 below its first-pass value. Otherwise, the comparison remains unresolved and is excluded from the detection counts.

For each comparison, we retain the input configurations, random seeds, code revision, sampled parameter vectors, optimized likelihoods, and numerical checks. The records also identify the source template and PSF kernels by their hashes, linking each reported statistic to its inputs and fitting procedure.
